chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya narrated from Ubayd Allah ibn Ahmad, from al-Hasan ibn Mahbub, from al-'Ala', from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) who said:

"If the authority were ours, we would accept the testimony of a single man if goodness was known from him, along with the oath of the opposing party, in the rights of people. As for what is from the rights of God or the sighting of the crescent, then [it is not accepted]."
ai.seo_question: What is the difference between accepting single testimony for civil rights versus divine rights in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes a pragmatic legal principle where the testimony of a single just man (shahadat al-rajul al-wahid), coupled with the opponent's oath, suffices for civil rights (huquq al-nas), reflecting the flexibility of Shia jurisprudence in commercial and personal disputes. However, this leniency is explicitly excluded for divine rights (huquq Allah) and specific evidentiary markers like sighting the lunar crescent, which require stricter, often multiple, witnesses to ensure communal certainty and ritual accuracy.
